item.text: {"question_id":"5B.8","answer":"Distributional policy was mixed and only partly assessable in actual incidence during 2023. The federal government implemented Bürgergeld, expanded Wohngeld, increased BAföG support, and launched income-qualified family housing loans; these measures were designed to support lower-income households, but the supplied evidence does not establish comprehensive take-up or realized incidence (BATCH-0026-E007; BATCH-0024-E008; BATCH-0020-E007; BATCH-0027-E003). DIW modeling indicates that social transfers, energy transfers, and gas-market stabilization supported lower-income households more than higher-income households, while tax relief favored higher-income households; its estimate placed relief at about 0.2% of GDP for lower-income groups versus about 0.5% for higher-income groups. These are modeled effects, not observed long-term incidence (BATCH-0034-R12-E004; BATCH-0034-R12-E006). DIW separately reported that the inflation-compensation tax law mainly benefited top earners, provided little or nothing to low-income people, and that the promised climate benefit had not been paid (BATCH-0025-E017). The same period also saw unequal burdens: inflation and weak wage growth especially harmed low-income households, while cumulative real-wage losses remained; DIW’s later 2023 assessment that effective wages rose particularly strongly at the bottom and that inequality likely did not rise substantially was a model-based nowcast, not a final incidence measure (BATCH-0025-E016; BATCH-0035-E007). Independent distributional indicators remained adverse or uneven: lower-income household incomes stagnated relative to average real incomes, poverty risk was elevated among single parents, children, migrants, lower-education households, and especially single or divorced women, while 2023 child-poverty measures principally used prior-year income and cannot be treated as wholly realized 2023 policy outcomes (BATCH-0009-E006; BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0024-E001; BATCH-0024-E002). Group and regional disparities were also documented. Asylum-seeker benefits were below regular social benefits, with disputed calculation differences and substantial local and Länder discretion; access to work was delayed or discretionary, especially in reception centres and for some national-origin categories; school access varied by state and could be delayed; and specialized psychosocial support was severely constrained, with a federal funding-cut proposal later reduced but affecting an already inadequate system (BATCH-0011-R04-E009; BATCH-0011-R04-E016; BATCH-0011-R04-E018; BATCH-0011-R05-E001). Gender pay disparities and uneven shelter access persisted, including a reported 18% average gross hourly wage gap in 2022 and a 15,000-place shelter shortfall, though those indicators partly predate 2023 (BATCH-0009-E017). Overall, there is material evidence of targeted lower-income support and some modeled progressive effects, but also regressive tax incidence, persistent class, gender, migrant, asylum-seeker, and regional disparities, and incomplete implementation and take-up evidence. Attribution is institutional and mixed: federal policy is identifiable for several measures, while Länder and local administration, markets, inflation, inherited inequality, and external conditions materially shaped actual incidence; the supplied evidence does not establish personal Scholz attribution for most
